title: The Seamstress's Room and the Avenue George V: a Basque tailor in the century of Paris
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Getaria, birth on the fishing coast
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Getaria stands on a rock above the Bay of Biscay, a whaling and fishing town of the Gipuzkoan coast with its church built over the road and its harbour open to the north. On the twenty-first of January a son is born to José Balenciaga Basurto, mariner, and Martina Eizaguirre Embil, seamstress, and is christened Cristóbal. The town's trade is the sea. The house's other trade is the needle, and it is the needle the boy inherits. Seventy-seven years later he is carried up the hill behind this town and buried in sight of the same water.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of Getaria, Gipuzkoa, for January 1895
sources: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline essay on Balenciaga

stops.name: Getaria, the mariner is gone
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source reached; placed in his early childhood, ahead of the seamstress's-room stop and well before the 1907 apprenticeship, for sequence only
stops.campa: The father dies while the son is still a child. No source reached gives the year and none gives the cause; the biographies keep the fact and drop everything around it. What is left is a household of a widow and her children living on what a seamstress can earn in a town of fishermen. Martina Eizaguirre keeps them by sewing, for the households of the town and for the palace above it. Cristóbal is small enough that the room where she works is the room where he is kept, and her hands are the first work he watches closely.
suggested_refs: The fishing fleet of Getaria, the trade Balenciaga did not enter

stops.name: Getaria, the seamstress's room
stops.date_confidence: undated; a sequence placement in his early childhood
stops.campa: Martina Eizaguirre Embil sews for the households of the town and for the great house above it. The boy sits in the room while she works and watches cloth pinned and cut. Nothing in Getaria suggests a career in this. A seamstress is a trade, not a calling, and the fishing coast has no couture. What he takes from the room is that a garment is built rather than drawn. Every account of his life starts there, hostile or devoted, because there is nothing earlier on the record to start from.
suggested_refs: EISA, the house name he later cut from Eizaguirre, his mother's surname

stops.name: Getaria, the Aldamar Palace
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the museum's account gives no date and popular biography gives circa 1905
stops.campa: Above the town stands the Aldamar Palace, the Getaria residence of the Marquesa de Casa Torres, for whom Martina Eizaguirre sews. The boy begins learning dressmaking inside it, among clothes made in Paris and worn by a woman who orders them. Tradition goes further: the Marquesa saw his talent, took him up, and paid for his training in Madrid. The museum that holds his archive stops short of that claim. The house and the access are documented. The patronage is what the story has added since.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Aldamar at Getaria, beside which his museum now stands
sources: Cristóbal Balenciaga Museoa, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga: The Early Years' (Google Arts & Culture)

stops.name: Getaria, apprenticed at twelve
stops.date_confidence: attested to circa age twelve; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: Around his twelfth year he is bound apprentice to a tailor. The tailor's name is in no source reached, and neither is the shop. The apprenticeship teaches him to cut, to assemble, and to sew a garment entire with his own hands, in the way a provincial tailor must, because in a town this size there is nobody else to do any part of it. He is doing the whole of the work at twelve. Fifty years later Coco Chanel will say he is the only couturier left in Paris who can still do all three.
suggested_refs: The tailoring trade of small-town Gipuzkoa, c. 1907, where a man makes the whole garment

stops.name: Madrid, the training the tradition credits
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source reached; placed between the apprenticeship and the 1917 atelier for sequence
stops.campa: He goes to Madrid for formal tailoring training, and here the record thins into tradition. No date survives, no school is named, and who paid for it is exactly the claim that popular biography asserts and the archive does not carry. He arrives in the capital as a Basque tailor's apprentice and leaves it able to open a house of his own at twenty-two. Madrid will hold a studio of his for four decades, and he will close it on the same day he closes Paris.
suggested_refs: Madrid as a recurring atlas node, pinned in sarmiento.journey.json and serrano.journey.json

stops.name: San Sebastián, the atelier at 2 Calle Vergara
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1917 by the museum that holds his archive; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: At twenty-two he opens his own atelier at 2 Calle Vergara in San Sebastián, the summer capital where the Spanish court and its aristocracy take the season. The clients are at hand and the competition is Paris, which those clients visit. Spanish Wikipedia dates this house to 1919 and calls it Eisa. The museum that holds his archive dates it to 1917 and gives it no such name, and the V&A counted a centenary from 1917 when it built its retrospective. The atelier is his, and it is the first.
suggested_refs: 2 Calle Vergara, San Sebastián, site of the first Balenciaga house
sources: Cristóbal Balenciaga Museoa, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga: The Early Years' (Google Arts & Culture)
Victoria & Albert Museum, 'Balenciaga: Shaping Fashion' (2017), dated to the centenary
Forbes (2024), 'How Cristóbal Balenciaga Became The Master Of All Haute Couture'

stops.name: San Sebastián, Martina Robes et manteaux
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1927; day defaulted
stops.campa: Ten years on he opens a second establishment and calls it Martina Robes et manteaux: his mother's name set inside a French phrase, for a clientele that reads French on a label as a guarantee. The house he built alone now has a second address. He is thirty-two. In a century where couture means Paris, a Spanish house sells itself by sounding French. Basque cutting, Spanish clients, French lettering on the door: the label is aimed at Paris twenty years before he shows anything there.
suggested_refs: Martina Robes et manteaux, San Sebastián, March 1927
sources: Cristóbal Balenciaga Museoa, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga: The Early Years' (Google Arts & Culture)

stops.name: San Sebastián, EISA Costura shows its first collection
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of September the second house presents its first collection. That October it is renamed EISA Costura, the syllable cut out of Eizaguirre, and every Spanish branch he opens afterwards carries the name of his mother. This is where the name comes from and this is when: ten years after the first atelier, not at its founding. The error sits in the reference works and has been copied outward from them. EISA is the second house. The first had no name but his own and opened in 1917.
suggested_refs: EISA Costura, San Sebastián, renamed October 1927
sources: Cristóbal Balenciaga Museoa, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga: The Early Years' (Google Arts & Culture)

stops.name: Madrid, the second city
stops.date_confidence: the expansion is attested, the date is not; placed in the early thirties for sequence
stops.campa: EISA opens in Madrid. No source reached dates it, and the branch is recorded only as part of an expansion following the San Sebastián houses. What it gives him is the court and the aristocracy in their own capital rather than at their summer resort, the same women dressed in two cities across the year. The Madrid studios will run for the rest of his working life and will not outlast the Paris salon by a single day. On the first of July 1968 both shut together.
suggested_refs: The EISA studios of Madrid, closed 1 July 1968

stops.name: Barcelona, the third house
stops.date_confidence: the expansion is attested, the date is not; placed before the Civil War for sequence
stops.campa: EISA opens in Barcelona, the third Spanish city and the one whose money is made in industry rather than land. By the middle of the thirties Balenciaga dresses Spain out of three houses, and the nobility orders from him, including the family of the Marquesa in whose palace he first handled cloth. He is forty years old and has never shown a collection in Paris. Then the country his entire trade rests on begins to shoot itself, and the season stops happening.
suggested_refs: The EISA house of Barcelona, third of the Spanish branches

stops.name: San Sebastián, the war closes the shops
stops.date_confidence: the Civil War closure is attested without a date; the Paris move that follows is dated August 1937
stops.campa: The Civil War closes the Spanish shops. The clientele is a nobility in flight or in hiding. San Sebastián sits close to a front line, and there is no longer a season to sell into. Balenciaga does not wait the war out. He leaves for Paris, the city his own labels have been imitating in French since 1927, and arrives there a refugee of forty-two with a trade and no house. The Spanish branches reopen after the war and run until he shuts them himself.
suggested_refs: The Spanish Civil War on the Gipuzkoan coast, which emptied the San Sebastián season
sources: sansebastianturismoa.eus, on Balenciaga in San Sebastián

stops.name: San Sebastián, EISA reopens inside the new regime
stops.date_confidence: contradicted between sources and not resolved: the Vintage Fashion Guild dates the reopening to the end of the war in 1939, the balenciagatribute.com timeline reopens San Sebastián in 1938 with Madrid and Barcelona following at the war's end; day and month defaulted either way
stops.campa: The Spanish houses open again. San Sebastián first, then Madrid and Barcelona when the war ends, all three under the four letters cut from his mother's name. From this point until 1968 he runs couture inside Franco's Spain and couture in Paris at once, the same hands cutting for both, for thirty years. The departure of 1937 was not permanent, and the reference works that stop there describe an interruption as an exit. Whatever clientele the new order leaves standing walks back through these doors, and he is there to dress it.
suggested_refs: The EISA houses of San Sebastián, Madrid and Barcelona, trading from 1938 or 1939 until 1968
sources: Vintage Fashion Guild, 'Eisa' label resource ('when the war ended, in 1939, they reopened' and 'until it was closed in 1968')
balenciagatribute.com timeline (1938 reopening of San Sebastián, under the name EISA Costura)

stops.name: Paris, the House of Balenciaga is opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1937; day defaulted
stops.campa: In August he opens the House of Balenciaga in Paris. He is a foreigner in the one city that decides what clothes mean, arriving in the year of the Exposition and two years before the war, and he opens anyway. The street he chooses is lined with houses that trained their own designers from adolescence inside their own workrooms, and he arrives already forty-two, having learned the trade entirely somewhere else. What he brings is not a Paris training. It is a provincial tailor's entire hand, which Paris has largely stopped teaching.
suggested_refs: The canonical atlas Paris pin, 48.8566 / 2.3522, inherited here from roland_barthes.journey.json

stops.name: Paris, number 10 avenue George V
stops.date_confidence: address attested; the coordinate is inferred from the street's numbering, which runs from the Alma end
stops.campa: The salon is at number 10 avenue George V, near the Alma end of the street, in the eighth arrondissement where couture keeps its addresses. He works from it for thirty-one years and is almost never photographed inside it. The house shows, the buyers come, and the man who cuts stays behind the door. Paris will call him the mystery man before it calls him anything else, and for a quarter of a century the address is the only fixed fact about him that a newspaper can print.
suggested_refs: 10 avenue George V, Paris VIII, the salon from 1937 to 1968
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Avenue George V' (street geometry and numbering)

stops.name: Paris, the death of Wladzio d'Attainville
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of December Wladzio Jaworowski d'Attainville dies. He is the Franco-Polish businessman who has been Balenciaga's partner in the house and his partner in life since the twenties, and the workroom knows exactly what he is. Elisa Erquiaga, who sews there, puts it plainly long afterwards and without embarrassment. Balenciaga is fifty-three, at the opening of the decade in which he will do all of his most radical work. The house shows again in the new year.
stops.quote: [D'Attainville] was very handsome and well-educated and we all knew, but nobody spoke about it in the studio.
stops.quote_source: Elisa Erquiaga, Balenciaga dressmaker, quoted in V&A Blog, 'Balenciaga: Love and Hats!'
suggested_refs: 'Wladzio d'Attainville and the House of Balenciaga (1924-1948)', Costume (2026)
sources: Euppublishing, Costume (2026), 'Wladzio d'Attainville and the House of Balenciaga (1924-1948)'

stops.name: Paris, the collection said to be all black
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the mourning collection is a retrospective legend rather than an event, dated here to the season after the death for sequence
stops.campa: The story the trade tells is that the collection following d'Attainville's death was designed entirely in black, a whole season of mourning hung on the rails. The press archives of those months do not support it. The collections that follow carry vivid colour alongside the black pieces. The legend survives because it is the shape grief ought to take in a house whose founder never once explained himself in public. It is recorded here as legend; the death underneath it is not.
suggested_refs: The Paris fashion press of spring 1949, against which the all-black legend fails
sources: Wikipedia, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga' (carries the legend as fact)
period press archives cited in the verification pass (contradicting it)

stops.name: Paris, the waist removed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1951; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: He widens the shoulder and takes away the defined waist. Dior's New Look of four years earlier had put the waist back at the centre of the female body and pulled it tight; Balenciaga now removes the centre. The dress stops describing the woman inside it and stands off her, and the space between cloth and body becomes the thing he is designing. Everything he cuts for the next ten years follows from that subtraction, while the rest of the trade is still arguing about waists.
suggested_refs: The 1951 Balenciaga silhouette, held in the V&A and the Balenciaga Museoa collections

stops.name: Paris, the tunic dress
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: The tunic dress: a straight fall of cloth from shoulder to below the hip, worn over a narrow skirt, with no seam at the waist to say where the woman divides. Balenciaga cuts it himself in a workroom where the toiles are corrected on living models and the sleeve is set by his own hand. He is sixty and has been cutting since he was twelve. He never delegated the sewing, which is why he can build a shape he would not be able to draw, and why a toile goes back to his hands rather than to a sketch.
stops.quote_source: Cristóbal Balenciaga, quoted in Victoria & Albert Museum, 'Introducing Cristóbal Balenciaga'
suggested_refs: The 1955 tunic dress, forerunner of the waistless line

stops.name: Paris, the calendar broken
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1956; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: He moves his shows to a month after everyone else's. The couture calendar exists so that buyers and press can travel once and see a whole season, and stepping outside it means making the world come back a second time for one house. The reason given is that copyists were reproducing his work before his own clients could wear it. The effect is that Balenciaga stops competing inside the season and becomes its afterword, seen alone, with nothing hanging beside him for comparison.
suggested_refs: The Paris couture calendar of the 1950s and the copyist trade it fed

stops.name: Paris, the sack, the balloon, the baby doll
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1957; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: In one year he shows the high-waisted baby doll, a cocoon coat draped away from the back, the balloon skirt, and the sack dress, which has no waist at all. The British press, which reads clothes as an argument about women, answers at once and in the register of the tabloid. The sack is copied within a season by houses that laughed at it, and the silhouette hanging in every high street by 1958 has his cut inside it and another name sewn into the neck.
stops.quote: It's hard to be sexy in a sack!
stops.quote_source: Daily Mirror, quoted in Victoria & Albert Museum, 'Introducing Cristóbal Balenciaga'
suggested_refs: The 1957 sack dress and the British press reaction to it

stops.name: Paris, the chemise and Chanel's verdict
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1958; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: The chemise dress, waistless again, cut to hang from the shoulders and held by the trade to flatter any body put inside it. Coco Chanel, whose entire doctrine is that clothes should serve the woman wearing them, is contemptuous of what he does to necks and unreserved about the only thing that finally counts with her, which is whether a couturier can make a dress with his hands. Both of her judgements are on the record, made within a few years of each other, and neither cancels the other.
stops.quote: Balenciaga alone is a couturier in the truest sense of the word. Only he is capable of cutting material, assembling a creation and sewing it by hand, the others are simply fashion designers.
stops.quote_source: Coco Chanel, quoted in Victoria & Albert Museum, 'Introducing Cristóbal Balenciaga'
suggested_refs: The 1958 chemise dress; and Chanel's two opposed judgements, in the V&A article and the V&A blog

stops.name: Paris, Knight of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1958; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: France makes the Spaniard a Knight of the Legion of Honour. He has lived in the country twenty-one years, has given no interview, does not appear at the end of his own shows, and does not attend the parties where couture conducts its business. The state honours him regardless, because by 1958 the shape of the French season is decided in a workroom on the avenue George V and everybody in the industry knows it, including the government handing out the ribbon.
suggested_refs: The Légion d'honneur register for 1958

stops.name: Paris, the Empire line
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1959; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: The Empire line: the waist raised to just under the breast, the skirt falling free from there, a silhouette lifted out of the decade after the French Revolution and handed back to a Paris that has spent the fifties arguing about waists. In four years he has moved the waist up, moved it down, and abolished it. Christian Dior has been dead two years. The sentence he left about who conducts the trade has stayed attached to Balenciaga ever since, and is quoted more often now than any dress either man cut.
stops.quote: Haute couture is like an orchestra whose conductor is Balenciaga. We other couturiers are the musicians and we follow the direction he gives.
stops.quote_source: Christian Dior, quoted in Victoria & Albert Museum, 'Introducing Cristóbal Balenciaga'
suggested_refs: christian_dior: queued in QUEUE.md, no journey file yet, so the tribute has no file to point back to

stops.name: Brussels, the wedding dress of Fabiola de Mora y Aragón
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1960; day and month defaulted, the sources reached give only the year
stops.campa: Fabiola de Mora y Aragón marries Baudouin, King of the Belgians, in a gown made in Paris by Balenciaga and worn in Brussels. She is Spanish nobility and he is the couturier the Spanish nobility has used since San Sebastián; the dress travels north to a cathedral and is photographed by the world. He does not appear beside it. The most public garment of his career is worn in a building he is not standing in, by a bride whose face is on every front page while his is on none.
suggested_refs: The Fabiola wedding gown, 1960, held by the Belgian royal collection

stops.name: Madrid, the dictator's wife in a Balenciaga gown
stops.date_confidence: 1960 is the date carried in the title of the Cortezo watercolour, which is the firmest dating found; day and month defaulted, and the Madrid pin is the atlas's inherited Madrid coordinate rather than an attested location for any fitting
stops.campa: Carmen Polo de Franco, wife of the Caudillo, is dressed by Balenciaga. A watercolour by Víctor María Cortezo records her in one of his gowns and dates it to 1960, which is the firmest date the record gives for the relationship. The trade press puts her among his clients before the Second World War and cites nothing for it; the Spanish houses were shut through most of those years. Her daughter Carmen Franco y Polo is called one of his most important clients. In twelve years he leaves retirement to cut the granddaughter's wedding dress.
stops.quote: Doña Carmen Polo de Franco vestida por Balenciaga. 1960
stops.quote_source: Title of a 1968 watercolour by Víctor María Cortezo, recorded in a MutualArt lot listing
suggested_refs: Víctor María Cortezo, 'Doña Carmen Polo de Franco vestida por Balenciaga. 1960' (watercolour, 1968), MutualArt lot record
El País (English), 'The hidden side of fashion's Cristóbal Balenciaga', 13 January 2024, whose body could not be fetched
sources: El País (English), 'The hidden side of fashion's Cristóbal Balenciaga' (13 January 2024): headline and metadata only, body unreachable
WWD, Hannah Malach, 'The History of Balenciaga' (31 May 2024), which dates the client relationship 'prior to World War II' without corroboration
MutualArt lot record for the Cortezo watercolour

stops.name: Paris, Dior names him the master
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source reached; no occasion, publication or year survives, placed mid-decade for sequence
stops.campa: Christian Dior, the most famous couturier alive and the man whose New Look Balenciaga has spent a decade dismantling, calls him the Master of us all. The remark carries no date in anything reachable: no occasion, no publication, no year. It survives because everyone repeated it. In 2013 Mary Blume takes it for the title of her book about his workrooms, and the V&A prints it with a capital M on the catalogue record of an opera coat, which is where it can actually be cited from.
stops.quote_source: Christian Dior, quoted in V&A Explore The Collections, Opera Coat, museum no. O1435930
suggested_refs: Mary Blume, 'The Master of Us All: Balenciaga, His Workrooms, His World' (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2013)
sources: V&A Explore The Collections, Opera Coat, museum no. O1435930
Mary Blume, 'The Master of Us All' (2013)
note: the V&A article 'Introducing Cristóbal Balenciaga' does NOT carry this phrase, though it is widely cited for it

stops.name: Paris, Givenchy at the master's door
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources reached; placed in the mid-fifties, when Givenchy's own house was newly open
stops.campa: Hubert de Givenchy, thirty years younger and running his own house a few streets away, attaches himself to Balenciaga and is taken seriously in return. What he takes from it is a discipline of subtraction, and he repeats it for the rest of his life in nearly the same words each time. He will be standing in Getaria in June 2011, eighty-four years old, when the museum opens: one of the last men alive who watched those hands work and could say what they refused to do.
stops.quote: Balenciaga taught me everything I know. He taught me to care for the details, that it was not necessary to sew on a button where it had no use, or to add a flower to make a dress beautiful... no unnecessary detail.
stops.quote_source: Hubert de Givenchy, quoted in Grazia Magazine, '5 fascinating facts you didn't know about Hubert de Givenchy'
suggested_refs: Grazia Magazine, '5 fascinating facts you didn't know about Hubert de Givenchy' (which prints 'that is was', an evident typo)
sources: Grazia Magazine, '5 fascinating facts you didn't know about Hubert de Givenchy'
Wikipedia, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga' (Givenchy at the 2011 museum opening)

stops.name: Paris, what the other two said about him
stops.date_confidence: both remarks are undated in the sources reached; placed at the height of his reputation for sequence
stops.campa: Dior on the workroom: with fabrics, we do what we can, Balenciaga does what he wants. Chanel on the man: he dislikes women and dresses them so as to expose the wrinkles in their necks. The two remarks come from the two people best placed to judge him and they agree on nothing except that he is doing something the rest of them cannot do. He answers neither of them, in public or anywhere the record can find. His own statement of the matter puts the dress ahead of the woman.
stops.quote: A woman has no need to be perfect or even beautiful to wear my dresses, the dress will do that for her.
stops.quote_source: Cristóbal Balenciaga, quoted in V&A Blog, 'Balenciaga: Love and Hats!'
suggested_refs: V&A Blog, 'Balenciaga: Love and Hats!', which carries both the Chanel hostility and his own reply
sources: 10 Magazine, 'Ten Quotes: Cristóbal Balenciaga's Enduring Legacy'

stops.name: Paris, the mystery man photographed against his will
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1962; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: France-Soir prints a stolen photograph of him in his white work smock and captions it: this is Balenciaga, the mystery man. He has been working in Paris twenty-five years and has given no interview to anyone. The picture is news because the face is news, which is precisely the result the silence has produced. Prospect will later record that in a career of half a century he gave two interviews and no more, and in 1962 he has not yet given the first of them.
stops.quote: This is Balenciaga, the mystery man.
stops.quote_source: France-Soir caption, 1962, cited in Forbes (2024), 'How Cristóbal Balenciaga Became The Master Of All Haute Couture'
suggested_refs: The France-Soir photograph of 1962, the first published image of him at work
sources: Forbes (2024), 'How Cristóbal Balenciaga Became The Master Of All Haute Couture'
Prospect Magazine (which states he gave only two interviews)

stops.name: Paris, Barthes reads the fashion press instead of the clothes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Roland Barthes publishes Système de la mode, built not from garments but from what magazines write about garments, a structuralist grid laid over the written dress. Three years earlier his Éléments de sémiologie had promised to take signifier and signified and apply them to clothes, food, furniture, cars. He is working in the same city, in the same decade, on the language of the thing Balenciaga makes with his hands. Nothing attests that the two men ever met. Barthes's fashion has no fabric in it.
suggested_refs: roland_barthes.journey.json, the stop 'Paris, Système de la mode' (1967), and its Éléments de sémiologie stop of 1964
sources: note: no meeting between Barthes and Balenciaga is attested anywhere; the link is co-location and subject matter only

stops.name: Paris, the last collection
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1968; day defaulted
stops.campa: He shows in January for the last time, and nobody in the room is told that is what it is. Around him Cardin, Courrèges, Saint Laurent and Ungaro have all moved into ready-to-wear, where the money now is and where a garment is designed once and reproduced by machine in thousands. The workroom he keeps is the other thing entirely: hand cut, hand sewn, fitted to one living body. The two cannot be the same trade, and he has already decided which one he was in.
suggested_refs: FIT, 'Paris Refashioned, 1957-1968: 1968 The End of True Couture?'
sources: FIT, 'Paris Refashioned, 1957-1968: 1968 The End of True Couture?'

stops.name: Paris, the retirement announced
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1968; day defaulted
stops.campa: In May he announces that he is finished. The reason he gives is neither age nor money. It is that the work can no longer be done: the seamstresses are leaving for the factories, the clients who ordered forty pieces a year are down to four, and a silhouette is copied off a runway inside a fortnight. He is seventy-three, and he shuts the house rather than change what it makes. It is the only public statement of principle he ever makes, and he makes it by closing a door.
stops.quote_source: Cristóbal Balenciaga, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga', cited as his justification for closing his house
suggested_refs: The May 1968 announcement, made in the month Paris was on strike

stops.name: Paris and Madrid, the couture operations shut
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of July the couture operations close: the headquarters on the avenue George V, and the Madrid studios that carry his mother's name in four letters. The perfume and accessories divisions continue, because a name is an asset and can be sold on separately from the hands that made it worth anything. The workrooms are emptied and the cutters are let go. The house of Balenciaga survives the closing of Balenciaga's house, and is still trading under the name half a century later.
suggested_refs: The EISA studios of Madrid and the Paris salon, closed the same day

stops.name: Paris, the first interview of his life
stops.date_confidence: the sources date the Paris Match interview to 1968 without a month; the stop is placed after the 1 July closure because that is where the reporting puts it, so the day and month here are a sequence placement and not an attestation
stops.campa: He gives an interview to Paris Match. It is the first of his life, at seventy-three, in the year he stops working, and the only one he gives to a French publication. Thirty-one years of Paris couture stand behind it: the sack and the balloon and the Empire line, the Legion of Honour, the calendar bent around one house. Against all of that, one conversation with a magazine, given at the end. The house is shut. There is no longer a collection that an interview could damage.
suggested_refs: Paris Match, 1968, the first of his two interviews

stops.name: Madrid, advising the machine-makers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period between retirement and death; the pool dates it 1970 without a month
stops.campa: In retirement he collaborates informally with Spanish ready-to-wear companies, putting no money of his own into any of them. The sources do not name a single firm. The man who closed a couture house rather than let a machine make his clothes spends part of his last years telling people who make clothes by machine how it ought to be done. He takes no stake and signs nothing. Whatever he said in those rooms is not in any source reached, and is recorded here as missing.
suggested_refs: The unnamed Spanish prêt-à-porter firms he advised, c. 1970

stops.name: Madrid, the second and final interview
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1971, reported from Spain; day defaulted
stops.campa: He gives his second interview, to The Times, at the insistence of the journalist Prudence Glynn, who is his friend and will not be refused. It runs under the title Balenciaga and la vie d'un chien, a dog's life, which is his own description of the trade he gave fifty-four years to. It is the last thing he says in public. Two interviews in a career: 1968 and 1971, both after he had stopped working, both given at a point when there was nothing left to protect.
suggested_refs: Prudence Glynn, 'Balenciaga and la vie d'un chien', The Times, August 1971

stops.name: Madrid, the gown at El Pardo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes out of retirement to cut one more dress. Carmen Martínez-Bordiú, granddaughter of Francisco Franco, marries at the chapel of El Pardo on the eighth of March in a gown by Balenciaga. The refugee of 1937, who left Spain because a war had made his trade impossible, dresses the bride of the dictator's family in the dictator's own palace thirty-five years afterwards. It is the last piece of couture he makes. He is seventy-seven and has two weeks left.
suggested_refs: The chapel of the Palacio de El Pardo, Madrid, 8 March 1972
sources: 24 Horas Mundo, '50 years after his death, the brand is more hip than ever'

stops.name: Jávea, the heart fails at the Parador
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's original 22 March was off by one day
stops.campa: He is at the Parador in Jávea on the Alicante coast, with the designer Ramón Esparza, when his heart fails. The date is the twenty-third of March. Half the reference works give this day as the day of his death and half give the next, and both are describing the same two days from opposite ends. He is carried out of the hotel alive and taken north to Valencia. The Mediterranean is not his sea. The cold one at the other end of Spain is, and he will be carried back to it within days.
suggested_refs: The Parador de Jávea (Xàbia), Alicante, 23 March 1972

stops.name: Valencia, death at the Sanatorio de la Sagrada Familia
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia and the English biographical literature; es.wikipedia and several Spanish sources give 23 March and Jávea, and the contradiction is carried rather than merged
stops.campa: He is admitted to the Sanatorio de la Sagrada Familia in Valencia, suffers a second attack in intensive care, and dies in the early hours of the twenty-fourth of March, aged seventy-seven. English sources give the twenty-fourth and Valencia; Spanish sources often give the twenty-third and Jávea. Neither is wrong about what it is actually describing. The collapse is the twenty-third and in Jávea; the death is the twenty-fourth and in Valencia, and the record here keeps both dates and both places rather than forcing them into one.
suggested_refs: The Sanatorio de la Sagrada Familia, Valencia; and the two-date contradiction in the reference works
sources: Vanidades, 'De qué murió Cristóbal Balenciaga' (the reconciling sequence)

stops.name: New York, the trade paper prints three words
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Women's Wear Daily, the trade paper that covered every Paris season he ever showed, runs three words across its front page. In the same coverage it calls him the father of contemporary fashion and says the influence outlasts the man. He has been retired four years and absent from the newspapers for most of his life. The trade press writes about his death in the language monarchies use, which is the language his own workroom used about him while he lived.
stops.quote_source: Women's Wear Daily headline, 24 March 1972, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga'
suggested_refs: Women's Wear Daily, 24 March 1972
sources: Victoria & Albert Museum, 'Introducing Cristóbal Balenciaga' (for the WWD 'father of Contemporary fashion' line)

stops.name: Getaria, buried above the water
stops.date_confidence: the sources date the burial only to March 1972; the day here follows the death and is a placement, not an attestation
stops.campa: He is carried up to the cemetery of Getaria, on the hill above the town where he was born, and buried in sight of the Bay of Biscay. The mariner's son comes back to the fishing village from the avenue George V, seventy-seven years after the seamstress's room. Two weeks earlier he was in Madrid, cutting a wedding dress for the dictator's granddaughter. Getaria holds roughly the same number of people it held in 1895, and the boats still work out of the same harbour mouth. Nothing in the town, then or now, accounts for him.
suggested_refs: The cemetery of Getaria; Find a Grave memorial 14602094 (the coordinate is the cemetery, not a surveyed grave)

stops.name: Getaria, the museum opens beside the palace
stops.date_confidence: attested by the museum, spain.info, Tourism Euskadi and es.wikipedia; en.wikipedia dates the public opening to 10 June and the contradiction is left standing
stops.campa: The Cristóbal Balenciaga Museoa opens beside the Aldamar Palace, the house where a seamstress's son first handled cloth. Queen Sofía inaugurates it on the seventh of June, and Hubert de Givenchy stands there with her, eighty-four years old, the last of the couturiers who watched the man work. It is the first major museum in the world given over to a single couturier. English Wikipedia dates the public opening three days later; the museum and the Spanish sources give one date for both.
suggested_refs: Cristóbal Balenciaga Museoa, Getaria, adjoining the Palacio Aldamar

stops.name: Getaria, the archive counted
stops.date_confidence: the Foundation's published figures are current rather than dated; the date is a placement after the museum's opening
stops.campa: The Foundation holds more than twelve hundred garments and accessories inside an archive of more than three thousand pieces: sketches, toiles, swatches, letters, photographs. About ninety items hang at a time, so the collection is shown by rotation and most of it is always in the dark. A figure of five thousand five hundred circulates in the press and is supported by nothing the Foundation itself publishes. The clothes are stored in the town where he was born, a few hundred metres from the harbour.
suggested_refs: Cristóbal Balenciaga Foundation, 'Preserving and Sharing a Heritage' (Google Arts & Culture)
sources: Google Arts & Culture, 'Cristóbal Balenciaga Museum: Preserving and Sharing a Heritage'
note: the '5,500 items' figure carried by wwd.com timelines is unsupported and was dropped

stops.name: London, the dresses are x-rayed
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 2017; day defaulted
stops.campa: The Victoria and Albert Museum opens Balenciaga: Shaping Fashion, the first British retrospective, timed to a hundred years since the San Sebastián atelier and eighty since the Paris salon. About a hundred garments and twenty hats hang beside work by more than thirty designers who took from him. The show x-rays the dresses to show the construction underneath, which is now the only way to see what those hands did, since the hands are gone and the work was always on the inside.
suggested_refs: 'Balenciaga: Shaping Fashion', V&A, London, 2017
sources: Dezeen (2017), 'V&A celebrates legacy of fashion designer Cristóbal Balenciaga in new exhibition'

stops.name: Paris, the name without the man
stops.date_confidence: the advertising scandal is attested to 2022; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: The label has run since his death under Nicolas Ghesquière, Alexander Wang and Demna Gvasalia, and in 2022 it becomes the centre of an advertising scandal covered around the world. A name that belonged to a man who gave two interviews in fifty-four years now generates news continuously and on purpose. In January 2024 a Spanish miniseries dramatises the Paris years for Disney, puts Alberto San Juan's face on the mystery man, and takes back the one thing he had managed to keep.
suggested_refs: SSENSE, 'The A-Z Guide to Balenciaga'; and the Disney+ miniseries 'Cristóbal Balenciaga', released 19 January 2024
